title: You Have to Start Cleaning to Find the Dirt
author: Jo Lein
summary: Lein, an assistant principal, builds an essay on school leadership out of an afternoon spent cleaning her car in the Tulsa heat, where lifting one piece of paper revealed a cup holder worse than anything she had set out to clean. The transferable observation is that inquiry in schools is not neutral: pulling the attendance report, actually reading the student work, asking families why children are not arriving, or visiting enough classrooms to see a pattern all convert a vague unease into knowledge you now have to act on. She then turns on her own instinct to fix, noting that schools drill the see-the-problem-solve-the-problem loop and reward the visible satisfaction of vacuum lines. The sharper move is her distinction between not knowing what to do and knowing exactly what to do without the people, time or money to do it, and her claim that leaders routinely collapse the second into the first and start talking about effort, training, accountability measures and new spreadsheets while everyone involved is already scrubbing. From there she names what she calls the dangerous confusion of resourcefulness with resources, warning that educators who keep making impossible things work teach everyone that the conditions are workable. She refuses the opposite escape too, treating the system as another convenient piece of paper to lift rather than a place to file responsibility. Her resolution is modest and unsatisfying on purpose: better is not fixed, unfixed is not hopeless, and the work is to go back for another paper towel.
points: Looking closely at attendance, student work or classroom practice removes the option of not seeing, which is a cost of inquiry that school improvement talk rarely acknowledges.

She separates a capacity problem from a knowledge problem and argues that schools mislabel the first as the second, then respond with training and accountability aimed at people who are already working flat out.
The resourcefulness-versus-resources line is the essay's core claim: educators covering the gap indefinitely is the mechanism by which unworkable conditions get normalized.
She declines to let the system absorb all responsibility, treating that framing as its own piece of paper that needs lifting.
Her account of leadership ends in maintenance rather than resolution, accepting the gap between clear sight and actual power to fix.
quotes: There is a deeply satisfying feeling when you start making things right. There's that little dopamine hit when you finally clear the inbox you have been working on since 7 a.m., throw away the cups, or vacuum the little rows into the mats.
This likely resonates with those of you who have worked in educational leadership. Sometimes things look manageable until you really start looking.
But there is a part we do not talk about very much: Once you know, you know. And now you have to do something with it.
But what happens when you find the dirt and don't have what you need to clean it?
Sometimes we absolutely know the problem. We just do not have enough people. Or enough time. Or enough money. And that is different from not knowing what to do.
But I am starting to wonder whether one of the more dangerous things we do in schools is confuse resourcefulness with resources.
If we keep making impossible things work, eventually people start believing the conditions are workable.

I think that is the part of leadership I understand differently now. Seeing clearly does not always give you the power to solve what you see. Sometimes it just takes away your ability to pretend you do not see it, which is considerably less satisfying than vacuum lines.
